title: Ancient genomics study reveals low HLA diversity in eastern hunter-gatherers.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Queried the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, a public sequence repository) file report for PRJEB81456: it is open and real, but holds raw whole-genome-shotgun FASTQ reads (individual runs 0.02-2.2 GB; 84 libraries), which project rules forbid downloading. Fetched the GitHub repository onur-ozer/EHG-immunogenomics: it contains only three R scripts (frequency_plots.R, fst_pcoa.R, shannon_diversity.R) and an MIT LICENSE, no data files. Resolved all three Zenodo DOIs: 16555858 is the third-party PyPop software, 21197801/21197802 are the same code snapshot of the GitHub scripts. No dataset was retrievable in tabular form.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All sample and label counts (43 individuals sampled, 36 passing genome-wide genotyping, 31 HLA-enriched, 27 with HLA genotypes, 13 complete at all six loci) come from the article text. The supplementary workbook holding the actual HLA (human leukocyte antigen, the immune-recognition gene cluster) calls, Additional file 1 Table S1, could not be downloaded: Springer static content returned HTTP 403, the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out twice, and the PMC open-access package service returned 404. So I never saw a single HLA genotype row.

a1_downloadable.note: ENA accession PRJEB81456 is open with no login, and the comparison resources (Allen Ancient DNA Resource v54.1.p1 on Harvard Dataverse, 1000 Genomes HLA types, Allele Frequency Net Database) are public. But the one table that carries this paper's new labels (supplementary Table S1) was not retrievable by any allowed route: 403 from the publisher, repeated timeouts from Europe PMC, 404 from the PMC open-access service.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Per the text, HLA allele calls per individual are reported as columns of Additional file 1 Table S1, so the label would not need constructing. Unverified: I could not open that file.

a3_inputs_present.note: The only inputs deposited are raw FASTQ sequencing reads at ENA. Model-ready features (the 1,233,013-SNP pseudohaploid genotypes produced with SequenceTools) are not deposited anywhere I found; you would have to re-map reads and re-genotype 84 libraries yourself.

a4_units_stated.note: Labels are categorical HLA allele names at first- and second-field resolution (e.g. B*27:05), a standard nomenclature, so units are not an issue. From the paper text, not the file.

a5_enough_rows.note: KILLER. 27 individuals have HLA genotypes (only 13 complete at all six loci) and 36 have genome-wide genotypes. The checklist floor is ~400 rows for a classification task; this is roughly 15x short. Count from the paper text.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Individual ENA runs are up to 2.2 GB of compressed reads across 84 libraries, verified in the ENA file report. Getting from deposit to features needs read mapping, damage handling and HLA genotyping (TARGT, OptiType) - not a laptop working set, and far over the 50 MB download rule.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The text is internally consistent (84 skeletal elements, 43 individuals, 36 genotyped, 31 enriched, 27 typed) and I saw no contradiction, but I could not cross-check against a download because the supplement was unreachable.

a8_label_provenance.note: HLA calls come from targeted in-solution capture of the HLA region genotyped with the TARGT pipeline and cross-confirmed with OptiType - software calls, but on direct sequence of the genes themselves, i.e. a measurement rather than another model's prediction. Note the capture assay is a different assay from the genome-wide SNP panel, so no leakage by construction.

existing_models.name: HIBAG (HLA genotype imputation with attribute bagging, 2013)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported 92.2-98.1% accuracy for HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQB1 from common SNP-array markers; evaluated on held-out individuals from European-ancestry reference panels.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Accuracy for rare alleles and for non-European ancestries; a later West African evaluation (PLOS One 2023) found accuracy drops there.

existing_models.name: CookHLA (Nature Communications, 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Beat SNP2HLA and HIBAG; ~80% accuracy for alleles at 0.1-0.5% frequency in a European reference panel versus 40-60% for the older tools.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Imputation of rare alleles and populations without a matched reference panel.

existing_models.name: DEEP*HLA (deep learning HLA imputation, Nature Communications 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Highest accuracy of the compared methods on Japanese (n=1,118) and European (n=5,122) reference panels, with the biggest gains on low-frequency and rare alleles; held-out-individual cross-validation.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Dependence on reference-panel ancestry match; performance for very rare alleles.

existing_models.name: HLARIMNT (transformer-based HLA imputation, Journal of Human Genetics 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported consistently higher accuracy than the convolutional DEEP*HLA on the same reference panels; held-out-individual split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Imputation efficiency for infrequent alleles and the need for large reference datasets.

existing_models.name: prophaser (ancient-DNA low-coverage genotype imputation, Bioinformatics 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Better accuracy than Beagle-based ancient-DNA pipelines at low coverage, especially for rare variants; evaluated on downsampled modern and ancient genomes.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Divergence between reference haplotypes and the ancient study population, and unevenly distributed coverage.

backbone.name: None appropriate; HLA imputation uses reference-haplotype or small supervised models (HIBAG, DEEP*HLA), not a pretrained foundation model

integration.partner_dataset: Allen Ancient DNA Resource (AADR) v54.1.p1, ~16,000 ancient and present-day individuals genotyped at 1.23M SNPs, plus 1000 Genomes HLA types
integration.join_key: Genomic coordinates on human genome build hg19 / 1240K SNP positions; sample identifiers for the HLA tables
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does HLA allele imputation trained on modern reference panels stay accurate on ancient low-coverage genomes from populations with no matched modern reference - and this paper's 27 true ancient calls would be a test set, not a training set.

controls.positive_control: Would be: re-impute HLA types for the 1000 Genomes individuals whose true types are published (Abi-Rached et al. 2018) and recover the known accuracy.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling across individuals; ablating the MHC-region SNPs.
controls.external_validation: The 27 ancient HLA calls here, and the published ancient Neolithic-farmer HLA datasets the paper compares against - but 27 individuals is too few for a stable accuracy estimate.

honest_claim_h3: With only 27 ancient individuals (13 complete at six loci) from one burial complex, any model claim would be limited to 'this is what one small eastern hunter-gatherer community's immune-gene types look like' - a population-genetics observation, not a learnable mapping.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use ancient genome-wide SNP genotypes to predict each ancient individual's immune-recognition gene types.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on modern reference panels where both SNP genotypes and true HLA (human leukocyte antigen) types are known - 1000 Genomes, roughly 2,500 individuals - because this paper itself supplies only 27 labelled ancient individuals.
plain_idea.predict: Output is the pair of HLA alleles at each of six genes (HLA-A, -B, -C, -DPB1, -DQB1, -DRB1). The true answer here came from targeted DNA capture of the HLA region sequenced and called with the TARGT pipeline, cross-checked with OptiType.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Ancient-DNA labs want to know whether cheap SNP-based HLA imputation can replace expensive targeted capture on degraded samples; a clear answer would change how they budget immunogenetics studies. But this paper's 27 individuals can only test such a model, never train one.

more_or_better_data.why: 27 labelled ancient individuals against reference panels of 1,118-5,122 individuals used by DEEP*HLA and CookHLA. The only edge is the population (eastern hunter-gatherers), and 27 samples cannot support a model.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate HLA measurements per individual beyond TARGT-versus-OptiType concordance for class I, and 13-27 individuals is far too few to calibrate per-prediction uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: CookHLA (2021), DEEP*HLA (2021) and HLARIMNT (2024) are recent, open, and already evaluated on held-out individuals with honest rare-allele breakdowns; prophaser (2023) specifically covers ancient low-coverage imputation.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The precondition fails at the start: this paper adds 27 rows to a task whose published models train on thousands, and its model-ready SNP genotypes are not even deposited.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: impute HLA alleles from low-coverage ancient pseudohaploid SNP genotypes, training on modern panels and using this paper's 27 true ancient calls as external validation. The paper's own contribution is a 27-row validation set, not a training set, and the paper itself argues that SNP-panel-based HLA inference is unreliable for ancient samples because the 1240K panel is enriched for common variants and reverses the expected MHC diversity signal.

effort.compute_note: Working-set figure is from the ENA file report: single runs up to 2.2 GB of compressed FASTQ across 84 libraries, before mapping. No timings run because no usable tabular data was obtainable.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows with an HLA genotype. The paper states it in the abstract: 27. That single number kills the project before any download.

verdict_reason: A5 fails hard: 27 individuals with HLA genotypes (13 complete at all six loci) and 36 with genome-wide data, versus a ~400-row floor for classification. A3 and A6 also fail - the only deposit is raw whole-genome FASTQ at ENA, the model-ready SNP genotypes are not deposited, and the supplementary table carrying the labels was unreachable (403 from the publisher, repeated Europe PMC timeouts, 404 from the PMC open-access service). This is a fine population-genetics paper and a genuinely first-of-its-kind result, but it is a 27-sample observation, not an ML dataset; the adjacent task (HLA imputation) is already served by open, recently and honestly evaluated models (CookHLA, DEEP*HLA, HLARIMNT, prophaser).
